o: Simultaneously, every node x (except root) is re-parented to its closest ancestor y with s[y] == s[x], if one exists. Crucially, the new parents are decided based on the ORIGINAL tree's ancestry — 'simultaneously' means no cascading. After rewiring, report each subtree size. A DFS carrying 26 stacks (one per letter) of current-path ancestors finds each node's closest same-letter ancestor in O(1) amortized; then a reverse-order accumulation computes sizes.
k: Rewiring decisions depend only on the original tree, so one DFS with per-character ancestor stacks determines every node's new parent.
The closest same-letter ancestor of x is exactly the top element below x on the stack for letter s[x].
Subtree sizes after rewiring: initialize size=1 everywhere and, processing nodes in reverse DFS preorder, add each node's size into its NEW parent.

a.n: Approach 1: Iterative DFS with 26 ancestor stacks + reverse accumulation
a.i: During an iterative preorder, push each node onto the stack of its letter; the new parent is the element just beneath it on that stack (or its original parent if none). Reverse preorder guarantees children come before parents, so a single backward pass finishes the sizes.
s: Iterative DFS; on entering x push x to stacks[s[x]] and record newParent = second-from-top (else parent[x])
On exiting x, pop its letter stack
size[i]=1 for all i; iterate nodes in reverse preorder adding size[child] to size[newParent[child]]
a.t: O(n) — each node enters/leaves the DFS once and each stack operation is O(1)
a.sp: O(n) for stacks, order, and adjacency

w: The trap is treating the rewiring as sequential — example 2 shows node 2's new parent (node 1) is judged under the ORIGINAL tree where its parent was 4. Always compute all new parents from original ancestry, then aggregate sizes. Also note a node's new parent is always a proper ancestor in the original tree, so the final graph is still a tree rooted at 0. Follow-up: what if changes were applied sequentially/cascading? Then you'd need small-to-large merging or link-cut structures.
